user_language_aliases: Immediate or bright reverberation can mask consonants and reduce direct-to-reverberant contrast.

candidate_hypotheses.label: H1: The reverberant timing or reflection structure is the main cause
candidate_hypotheses.mechanism: Immediate or bright reverberation can mask consonants and reduce direct-to-reverberant contrast.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_needed: A current representative capture, exact insert/return scope, wet-only audition where useful, and matched-level full-mix comparison.
candidate_hypotheses.discriminating_test: Hold decay and level fixed, add pre-delay until consonants separate, then compare a darker or ducked return.

candidate_hypotheses.label: H2: The wet spectrum or dynamics is masking the source
candidate_hypotheses.mechanism: Low/high-frequency decay, sibilance, compression, saturation, or cumulative sends may create the complaint even if decay length is reasonable.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_needed: Wet-return spectrum/timeline as supporting evidence plus listening in the full arrangement.
candidate_hypotheses.discriminating_test: Keep timing fixed and change only wet-path filtering or dynamics, then restore it before the next test.

candidate_hypotheses.label: H3: The source or arrangement does not leave space for the effect
candidate_hypotheses.mechanism: Long sustain, dense instrumentation, performance phrasing, or section transitions may make any similar reverb cluttered.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_needed: Solo-versus-mix result, section comparison, and identification of which sources feed the return.
candidate_hypotheses.discriminating_test: Mute or reduce one competing send/source and compare before reshaping the reverb further.

candidate_hypotheses.label: H4: Routing, level, stereo, or monitoring is biasing the judgment
candidate_hypotheses.mechanism: Insert/send topology, duplicated dry signal, pre/post-fader behavior, width, room, headphones, or loudness mismatch may misrepresent the effect.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_needed: Routing inspection, matched-level bypass, mono check, and alternate monitoring where possible.
candidate_hypotheses.discriminating_test: Verify wet-only return and match level/width before changing the algorithm.

clarification_questions: What source or bus is receiving the effect, and is TrackSmith hearing that exact scope?
What are you trying to preserve: intelligibility, transient punch, groove, mono focus, realism, or an obvious creative effect?
Does the problem happen in solo, only in the full mix, or only in a particular section?
What routing, timing, feedback/decay, filtering, width, automation, and other processing are currently active?

recommended_first_experiment.summary: Hold decay and level fixed, add pre-delay until consonants separate, then compare a darker or ducked return.
recommended_first_experiment.action: Hold decay and level fixed, add pre-delay until consonants separate, then compare a darker or ducked return.
recommended_first_experiment.why_this_first: It is designed to distinguish the leading explanation from level, routing, spectrum, stereo, performance, arrangement, and monitoring alternatives before adding more processing.

rationale: The immediate issue is that immediate or bright reverberation can mask consonants and reduce direct-to-reverberant contrast. The first experiment changes one meaningful variable and produces causal information before a broader chain or preset is recommended.
logic_pro_steps: Loop a short representative passage that includes the busiest source interaction and at least one gap where the tail can be heard.
Save or note the current dry level, send amount, return level, plug-in preset, and relevant timing so the comparison can be undone exactly.
Hold decay and level fixed, add pre-delay until consonants separate, then compare a darker or ducked return.
Change only one timing, tone, routing, or level variable while keeping the dry source unchanged.
Match perceived loudness or wet contribution before judging whether the new version is clearer, deeper, wider, or simply louder.
Replay the full mix, a quieter section, and mono before keeping the change.
starting_points: Begin with the wet contribution at zero and raise it only until the intended spatial role becomes noticeable in context.
Use the shortest decay and least spectral width that still produces the required sense of space; extend only when the arrangement leaves room.
Treat pre-delay, filtering, early/late balance, and decay as listening orientations rather than universal numerical targets.
Judge the return at matched loudness and through the busiest section, not only while soloed.
what_to_listen_for: The direct source should keep its intended articulation, transient, lyric, pitch, or groove while gaining the requested space.
The tail should clear important later events rather than continuously filling every gap.
Listen for low-mid buildup, sibilant splash, metallic ringing, pumping, stereo instability, and loss of mono focus.
Check whether the improvement survives when the wet return is level-matched and the entire arrangement plays.
stop_rule: Stop or back off when the intended space improves but clarity, groove, tone, mono translation, or section contrast becomes worse.
stop_conditions: Stop or back off when the intended space improves but clarity, groove, tone, mono translation, or section contrast becomes worse.
undo_or_reset: Restore the saved send, return, reverb preset, timing, filtering, automation, and routing, then replay the same passage.
undo: Restore the saved send, return, reverb preset, timing, filtering, automation, and routing, then replay the same passage.
tradeoffs_and_risks: A louder or wider wet return can appear more impressive even when it reduces clarity.
Long, bright, or low-frequency tails can accumulate across phrases and consume headroom.
Pre-delay, width, modulation, compression, or filtering can change depth and tone in more than one way.
A source, performance, arrangement, or monitoring problem may be mistaken for a reverb-setting problem.
alternatives_if_wrong: Use a shorter room or early-reflection ambience instead of a longer tail.
Use a filtered delay, arrangement space, level automation, or source change instead of more reverb.
Print and edit a special tail as an arrangement asset when continuous live processing is hard to control.
common_mistakes: Copying a decay, pre-delay, feedback, note value, filter, or wet percentage without matching the source and arrangement.
Judging the effect soloed or louder than bypass.
Changing timing, tone, level, feedback, stereo mode, and routing simultaneously.
Using ambience or repeats to solve a performance, arrangement, balance, editing, or source-selection problem.
do_not_assume: A common setting, tempo formula, room label, or forum answer is correct for this source and song.
A spectrum, waveform, model observation, or plug-in label proves the artistic complaint or its cause.
More width, length, density, feedback, brightness, or wet level is automatically better.
The first plausible cause is the true cause.
teaching_principle: Reverb is control over the relationship between the direct sound, early reflections, and decaying field; choose the spatial cue and timescale that the arrangement can support.
